questions.prompt: Which set of characteristics describes a unit test?
options: Tests one function or class in isolation; fast and deterministic
Tests several services together through their real network APIs
Tests the full user journey through the UI on a staging system
Tests one class against a real database so results match production
Tests one function but may give different results on each run
questions.explanation: A unit test validates a single unit (function/class) in isolation with fast, deterministic, repeatable checks. Spanning services, the UI or a real database breaks isolation, and changing results contradict "deterministic".

questions.prompt: In the Red → Green → Refactor cycle of TDD, what is done in the green step?
options: Write the minimal code needed to make the failing test pass
Write a failing test that specifies the next behavior
Clean up the design while using the tests as a safety net
Write the complete design of the module before any code
Add tests for code that has already been fully implemented
questions.explanation: Green means making the failing test pass with minimal code. Writing the failing test first is the red step, and cleaning up with the tests as a safety net is the refactor step.

questions.prompt: In the step-by-step TDD workflow, how long should each cycle typically be kept?
options: About 2–10 minutes
Under 1 second
About 1–2 hours
About one working day
About one full sprint
questions.explanation: The workflow says to repeat and keep cycles short (2–10 min) to maintain momentum. Under 1 second is the target for running a local test suite segment, not for a TDD cycle.

questions.prompt: Which statement about TDD is correct?
options: It complements, rather than replaces, integration and E2E tests
It means writing the unit tests after the code is finished
It requires a complete, detailed design to be made up front
It is a form of end-to-end testing through the user interface
It works best with large units that are entangled with I/O
questions.explanation: TDD is not writing tests after coding, not full design up front and not end-to-end testing; it complements higher-level tests. Large units entangled with I/O are listed as a pitfall because they slow the cycles.

questions.prompt: In the comparison of Big Design Up Front and Emergent Design, which characteristic belongs to Emergent Design?
options: Assumes change is cheap
Think before you code
Supports governance
Requires abstract thinking
Fixes the design before coding
questions.explanation: Emergent Design assumes change is cheap, handles ambiguity and requires detail thinking. Thinking before you code, supporting governance and requiring abstract thinking are listed for Big Design Up Front.

questions.prompt: Among the limits and pitfalls of TDD, what does "test theater" mean?
options: Tests that produce coverage without adding real value
Tests that fail randomly because of time or concurrency
Tests that break because they over-specify internals
Tests that mock every collaborator and become fragile
Tests that run slowly because the units are too large
questions.explanation: "Test theater" is listed as coverage without value. Over-specifying internals, mocking everything and overly large units are separate pitfalls, and random failures from time or concurrency describe flaky tests.

questions.prompt: A class reads its configuration from a global static singleton, which makes it hard to unit test. Which change follows the design-for-testability guidance?
options: Inject the dependency through an interface or abstraction
Move the configuration into another global static variable
Merge the class and its dependencies into one larger unit
Make the singleton's fields public so tests can change them
Test it only end-to-end so the real singleton gets set up
questions.explanation: Designing for testability favors dependency inversion with interfaces/abstractions and clear seams for substituting dependencies, and says to avoid global state and static singletons that hide dependencies.

questions.prompt: A constructor requires a logger parameter, but the behavior under test never uses the logger. Which type of test double is intended for this case?
options: Dummy
Stub
Spy
Mock
Fake
questions.explanation: A dummy is passed but never used. Stubs return canned values, fakes are lightweight working implementations, spies record interactions and mocks verify them, none of which is needed here.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a mock from a stub?
options: A mock verifies interactions; a stub returns canned values
A mock returns canned values; a stub verifies interactions
A mock is passed but never used; a stub records interactions
A mock is a working in-memory version; a stub is never used
A mock records interactions only; a stub verifies call arguments
questions.explanation: A mock verifies behavior/interaction while a stub returns canned values. Being passed but never used describes a dummy, a lightweight working implementation is a fake, and recording interactions is a spy.

questions.prompt: Which dependency is the most appropriate to mock in a unit test?
options: An external HTTP service that the class calls
The project's own domain data model classes
The sorting algorithm the team implemented
A simple value object defined in the codebase
The system under test whose behavior is checked
questions.explanation: Mocking is recommended for external or hard-to-control dependencies such as I/O, time and HTTP. The course says not to mock your own data models or algorithms, and the system under test is exercised, not replaced.

questions.prompt: When using a mocking framework, why should mocks be reset or torn down between tests?
options: To keep state from leaking from one test into the next
To raise the statement and branch coverage of the suite
To verify how many times each method was called
To stub exceptions thrown by the mocked dependency
To set up given/when expectations for the next call
questions.explanation: Resetting/teardown isolates state between tests to avoid leakage. Verifying call counts, stubbing exceptions and arranging given/when expectations are separate mocking-framework patterns.

questions.prompt: In the Arrange–Act–Assert structure, what belongs to the Act phase?
options: Invoking exactly one behavior of the system under test
Creating the inputs, test doubles and system under test
Checking the resulting outcome or the interaction made
Resetting mocks so that no state leaks into later tests
Invoking several behaviors in a row to share one setup
questions.explanation: Act invokes one behavior; preparing inputs, doubles and the system under test is Arrange, and checking the outcome or interaction is Assert. Invoking several behaviors contradicts the one-behavior-per-test rule.

questions.prompt: You want to run the same test logic against many input values, including boundary values and representatives of each equivalence class, without copying the test. Which technique fits?
options: Parameterized tests driven by data sets
Mutation testing of the assertions
Smoke tests after promotion to staging
A canary rollout with gradual traffic
Spies that record every interaction
questions.explanation: Parameterized tests cover multiple cases with data sets and focus on boundary values and equivalence classes. Mutation testing measures how strong the tests are rather than adding input cases.

questions.prompt: A unit test fails intermittently because it uses the current system time and unseeded random numbers. Which fix matches the recommended approach?
options: Control the clock and seed the random number generator
Read the time from a real network time server instead
Run the test concurrently with others to expose timing
Move the test into the nightly end-to-end test suite
Raise the minimum coverage threshold in the pipeline
questions.explanation: Flakiness caused by time and randomness is fixed by controlling clocks and RNGs (seeds/clocks). Real networks and concurrency are themselves listed as causes of flaky tests, not fixes.

questions.prompt: A unit test suite reaches 95% branch coverage, but many tests only call methods and barely check the results. Which technique does the lecture suggest for exposing these weak assertions?
options: Mutation testing
Condition coverage
Smoke testing
Contract testing
Build matrices
questions.explanation: Statement/branch/condition coverage is useful but not a goal, because weak assertions can still yield high coverage; mutation testing is named as the way to catch them. Measuring another coverage criterion such as condition coverage only shows that more code ran, not that results were checked.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is listed as a test smell or anti-pattern?
options: Slow "unit" tests that touch real I/O
One behavior per test with a clear name
Seeding randomness to keep tests deterministic
Using fakes to keep tests realistic and fast
Arranging inputs and doubles before acting
questions.explanation: Slow "unit" tests touching real I/O are listed as a smell alongside over-mocking, testing private internals and giant copy-pasted setups. The other options are practices the course recommends.

questions.prompt: As a reason to automate testing, what does "shift-left" mean?
options: Catching issues earlier in the development process
Moving most testing to just before the production release
Running the test suite only in the production environment
Replacing most unit tests with a larger set of E2E tests
Waiting to automate tests until the code is fully stable
questions.explanation: Automation catches issues early, which is what "shift-left" means. Pushing testing toward release or production is the opposite, and replacing unit tests with E2E tests contradicts the testing pyramid.

questions.prompt: A team has 400 end-to-end tests, 60 integration tests and 20 unit tests, and feedback is slow. What does the testing pyramid suggest?
options: Have many fast unit tests, fewer integration and few E2E tests
Add more E2E tests, since they give the broadest confidence
Keep equal numbers of unit, integration and E2E tests
Replace the unit tests with integration tests against services
Remove all E2E tests and rely on unit tests alone
questions.explanation: The pyramid calls for many fast, cheap unit tests, fewer service/integration tests and few end-to-end tests to keep feedback quick. Integration/E2E tests are still used for cross-service confidence, so removing them all is wrong.

questions.prompt: After a trigger such as a push or PR, which order matches the high-level pipeline anatomy?
options: Build → Test → Analyze → Package → Deploy
Test → Build → Package → Analyze → Deploy
Build → Package → Deploy → Test → Analyze
Analyze → Build → Deploy → Package → Test
Build → Analyze → Deploy → Test → Package
questions.explanation: A pipeline triggers on push/PR/schedule, then runs Build → Test → Analyze → Package → Deploy, followed by feedback such as status checks, artifacts and notifications.

questions.prompt: Which activity belongs to the typical CD stages rather than the typical CI stages?
options: Smoke tests and health checks on staging
Checkout and dependency restore with caching
Linting and static analysis such as SAST
Unit tests run in parallel or as a matrix
Integration tests with services such as a DB or API
questions.explanation: CD promotes the build to staging, runs smoke tests and health checks, and gates promotion to production. Checkout, dependency caching, linting/static analysis, unit tests and integration tests are listed as CI stages.

questions.prompt: How does trunk-based development compare with GitFlow?
options: Trunk-based enables rapid integration; GitFlow offers stricter release control
Trunk-based offers stricter release control; GitFlow enables rapid integration
Both offer identical trade-offs, so choosing between them does not matter
Both are production deployment strategies, like canary and blue/green
Both remove the need for PR checks as quality gates before merging
questions.explanation: Trunk-based development enables rapid integration while GitFlow offers stricter release control. They are branching models with trade-offs, not deployment strategies, and PR checks are still used as quality gates.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of acronym and pipeline topic is correct?
options: SLSA – provenance of builds
SemVer – secrets scanning
SBOM – deployment strategy
SAST – artifact versioning
AAA – pipeline triggers
questions.explanation: SLSA basics are named together with build provenance. SemVer is for versioned artifacts, SBOM belongs to dependency scanning, SAST to static analysis/security checks, and AAA (Arrange–Act–Assert) to unit test structure.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of test type and typical CI timing is correct?
options: Performance and load tests – on a schedule or pre-release
Fast unit tests – only nightly, never on push
E2E/UI tests – on every push before linting
Contract/integration tests – only after production deploy
Performance and load tests – on every single push
questions.explanation: Fast unit tests run on every push, contract/integration tests on PRs or nightly, E2E/UI tests on staging or nightly, and performance/load tests on a schedule or pre-release to balance speed and depth.

questions.prompt: Which description of a deployment strategy is correct?
options: Rolling: updates instances in batches with health checks
Canary: switches all traffic instantly with easy rollback
Blue/green: gradual rollout driven by production metrics
Feature flags: tie each deployment directly to a release
Rolling: updates all instances at once without any checks
questions.explanation: Rolling updates change instances in batches with health checks. Blue/green gives an instant switch and easy rollback, canary is a gradual metrics-driven rollout, and feature flags decouple deploy from release.

questions.prompt: Which duration do the team best practices target for PR pipelines?
options: Under about 10 minutes
Under about 1 second
Under about 1 hour
Under about 4 hours
Under about 24 hours
questions.explanation: Best practices say to keep PR pipelines under about 10 minutes and to fail fast with clear, actionable messages. Under 1 second is the target for a local test suite segment, not a whole pipeline.

questions.prompt: In the red step of TDD, a new failing test specifies a behavior that has not been implemented yet. In the book's Venn diagram of specified (S), programmed (P) and tested (T) behaviors, where does this behavior lie at that moment?
options: In S and T, but not in P
In S and P, but not in T
In P and T, but not in S
In S, P and T
In T only, outside S and P
questions.explanation: The new test specifies and tests the behavior, but no code implements it yet, so it lies in S and T outside P (region 4 of the book's Figure 1.4), which is why the test fails. The green step adds the minimal code and moves the behavior into S, P and T (region 1).

questions.prompt: A developer new to a module learns how it is expected to behave by reading its TDD tests, which show concrete inputs and expected results. Which benefit of TDD does this illustrate?
options: Self-documenting examples that act as specs
Emergent design with better cohesion
Fewer regressions and safer refactoring
A complete design that is fixed up front
Coverage figures that rise without added value
questions.explanation: TDD leaves behind living examples that document expected behavior (self-documenting examples/specs). Emergent design and safer refactoring are other benefits that this scenario does not show, while a fixed up-front design and coverage without value (test theater) are not TDD benefits.

questions.prompt: Tests of an order service replace the real database with an in-memory implementation that actually stores and returns orders, so the tests stay realistic and fast. Which kind of test double is this?
options: Fake
Stub
Mock
Spy
Dummy
questions.explanation: A fake is a lightweight working implementation such as an in-memory DB, and the lecture prefers fakes to keep tests realistic and fast. A stub only returns canned values, a spy records interactions, a mock verifies them and a dummy is never used.

questions.prompt: A library must be built and tested on Windows, Linux and macOS, each with two SDK versions, on every pull request. Which CI infrastructure feature is meant for this?
options: A build matrix over OS and SDK versions
Caching of dependencies and Docker layers
A canary rollout with gradual traffic
A quarantine list for flaky tests
Feature flags that decouple deploy and release
questions.explanation: Build matrices run the same jobs across OS/SDK versions (here 3 × 2 = 6 combinations), and parallel jobs and matrices speed feedback. Caching only makes builds faster, while canary rollouts and feature flags are deployment and release techniques.

questions.prompt: A flaky test keeps blocking merges while its cause is being investigated. Which pipeline observability practice from the lecture addresses this?
options: Track the test and put it on a quarantine list
Raise the minimum coverage threshold for merges
Make the test a required PR quality gate
Run the test only in production after deploying
Roll back the last release with blue/green
questions.explanation: Observability in pipelines includes flaky test tracking and quarantine lists, because flaky tests blocking merges is a common CI/CD pitfall. The cause is then fixed separately, e.g. by controlling time and randomness.
